def: Small dark red to purple wart-like papules of dilated superficial capillaries with overlying thickened skin. Multiple lesions in a bathing-trunk distribution are classic for Fabry disease.
Lysosomal enzyme that degrades galactocerebroside and psychosine. Deficiency causes Krabbe disease.
Toxic lipid (galactosylsphingosine) that accumulates when galactocerebrosidase is deficient. Damages oligodendrocytes in Krabbe disease, causing demyelination.
Lysosomal enzyme that removes sulfate from sulfatides (cerebroside sulfate). Deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy.
Lysosomal enzyme that degrades heparan and dermatan sulfate. Deficiency causes Hurler syndrome.
Urea cycle disorder from arginase deficiency, causing progressive spastic paraplegia and high arginine, but usually milder hyperammonemia than other urea cycle defects.
Final urea cycle enzyme, hydrolyzing arginine to ornithine and urea in the liver. Deficiency causes hyperargininemia.
Mitochondrial enzyme making N-acetylglutamate, the activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Deficiency causes hyperammonemia.
Inherited deficiencies of urea cycle enzymes, causing hyperammonemia with vomiting, lethargy and encephalopathy. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is the most common.
Birth defects when a mother with untreated phenylketonuria has high phenylalanine in pregnancy. Causes microcephaly, intellectual disability, and heart defects in the fetus.
Enzyme in tyrosine breakdown that cleaves homogentisic acid. Deficiency causes alkaptonuria with dark urine and ochronosis.
Enzyme that incorporates both atoms of molecular oxygen into a substrate. Examples include homogentisate oxidase and lipoxygenase.
Product formed when S-adenosylmethionine donates its methyl group. Hydrolyzed to homocysteine and adenosine.
Rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine synthesis, converting tyrosine to L-DOPA. Requires tetrahydrobiopterin.
Mitochondrial enzyme in de novo pyrimidine synthesis that converts dihydroorotate to orotate. Inhibited by leflunomide.
Nucleotide carrying sugars in glycosylation and glycogen synthesis (UDP-glucose). Also precursor for pyrimidine nucleotides.
Enzyme that makes phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate from ribose-5-phosphate and ATP for purine and pyrimidine synthesis. Overactivity causes gout.
Enzyme converting IMP to XMP in guanine nucleotide synthesis. Inhibited by mycophenolate and ribavirin.
Enzyme converting guanine to xanthine in purine degradation, which is oxidized to uric acid.
Thiamine-dependent enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway transferring two-carbon units. Used to assess thiamine status.
Membrane proteins that carry amino acids across cell membranes. Defects cause Hartnup disease and cystinuria.
Test of vitamin B12 absorption using radiolabeled B12, with and without intrinsic factor, to distinguish pernicious anemia from other causes. Rarely used now.
Tendency of small vessels to rupture with minor stress, shown as petechiae in the tourniquet test. Seen in scurvy and platelet disorders.
Vitamin E, a fat-soluble antioxidant protecting cell membranes from lipid peroxidation. Deficiency causes hemolytic anemia and neuropathy.
Newborn bleeding from low vitamin K, as breast milk has little and the gut is sterile. Prevented by an intramuscular vitamin K injection at birth.
Distorted or unpleasant taste. Caused by zinc deficiency, drugs such as metronidazole and ACE inhibitors, and some infections.
Skin inflammation of the hands and feet and around orifices. Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a zinc deficiency disease.
Insufficient dietary calories and protein. Marasmus is wasting from overall deficiency, while kwashiorkor shows edema, ascites and fatty liver.
Synthesis of fatty acids and triglycerides, mainly in liver, from acetyl-CoA. Stimulated by insulin.
Short chains of a few amino acids, such as dipeptides and tripeptides, absorbed in the gut by PepT1.
Heme synthesis enzyme joining two ALA molecules to form porphobilinogen. Inhibited by lead.
Enzyme that removes water from a substrate, forming a double bond. Examples include ALA dehydratase and enolase.
Yellow pigment from urobilinogen oxidation that gives urine its color.
Drug that reduces sympathetic nervous activity, such as clonidine, alpha-methyldopa, or beta and alpha blockers.
Beta-2 agonist once used to delay preterm labor by relaxing uterine muscle. Largely abandoned because of maternal cardiac side effects.
Presynaptic protein reuptaking norepinephrine from the synapse. Blocked by cocaine, amphetamines and tricyclic antidepressants.
Part of the ventral striatum, a central part of the brain's reward pathway. Receives dopamine from the ventral tegmental area and is involved in addiction.
Protein packing dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin into synaptic vesicles. Reserpine and tetrabenazine inhibit it.
Nonselective beta blocker with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (partial agonist). Causes less bradycardia.
Listening to the heart sounds and murmurs with a stethoscope.
Iron deficiency anemia with dysphagia from esophageal webs and glossitis. Increases risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus.
Normal adult hemoglobin, two alpha and two beta chains. Makes up about 97 percent of adult hemoglobin.
Initial RNA transcript from DNA, before introns are removed, a 5' cap added and a poly-A tail attached.
Treatment with agents that bind metals and promote their excretion. Used for lead, iron, copper, and arsenic poisoning.
Anemia in which red cells have decreased hemoglobin and look pale. Seen in iron deficiency, thalassemia and sideroblastic anemia.
Tendency of red cells to lyse in hypotonic solution. Increased in hereditary spherocytosis.
Cell surface protein attached by a GPI anchor that blocks assembly of the membrane attack complex. Deficiency causes complement-mediated hemolysis in PNH.
Lipid anchor attaching some proteins to the outer cell membrane. Defective synthesis causes PNH.
Complement protein cleaved to C5a, a chemotactic anaphylatoxin, and C5b, which starts the membrane attack complex. Targeted by eculizumab.
Error-free repair of DNA double-strand breaks using the sister chromatid as a template. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are key.
Mast cell stabilizer inhaled or used in eye drops that blocks degranulation. Used for allergic conjunctivitis.
Midline embryonic mesodermal rod that induces the neural plate. Its remnant forms the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs.
Small posterior part of the diencephalon containing the pineal gland and habenula.
Centrally acting muscle relaxant metabolized to meprobamate, with abuse potential. Used for acute musculoskeletal pain.
Degeneration of the axon distal to an injury, with myelin breakdown and macrophage clearance. Allows regeneration in peripheral nerves.
Degenerative changes in the proximal axon and cell body after an injury. Includes chromatolysis, cell swelling and nucleus displacement.
Dural venous sinus along the top of the falx cerebri, draining CSF through arachnoid granulations. Thrombosis causes raised pressure and venous infarcts.
Paired dural venous sinuses running along the occipital bone that drain into sigmoid sinuses.
Neurons that connect other neurons within the CNS, usually inhibitory in local circuits.
Downward displacement of cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum. Type II includes myelomeningocele, hydrocephalus and brainstem herniation.
Cell surface receptors that bind the Fc portion of antibodies, mediating phagocytosis and cytotoxicity.
Deep space behind the maxilla containing the maxillary nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion and maxillary artery. Communicates with the orbit and nasal cavity.
Smallest major salivary gland beneath the tongue, supplied by the facial nerve through the submandibular ganglion.
Enzyme marker of osteoclasts, hairy cells and some macrophages. Positive staining diagnoses hairy cell leukemia.
Widespread redness and scaling of more than 90 percent of the skin. Causes include eczema, psoriasis, drugs and lymphoma.
Surgical interruption of sympathetic nerve supply. Used for hyperhidrosis and vasospastic conditions.
Varicella-zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, causing ear vesicles, facial paralysis and hearing loss.
Three tiny middle ear bones (malleus, incus, stapes) that transmit sound from the tympanic membrane to the oval window.
Middle ear bone between the malleus and stapes. Called the anvil.
Gel-like structure overlying hair cells in the organ of Corti. Stereocilia bend against it when the basilar membrane vibrates.
Transmission of sound through skull vibrations to the cochlea, bypassing the middle ear. Basis of the Weber and Rinne tests.
Cochlear ganglion containing bipolar neurons whose axons form the cochlear nerve.
Gelatinous layer with calcium carbonate crystals (otoliths) over hair cells in the utricle and saccule, sensing linear acceleration and head tilt.
Reflex moving the eyes opposite head movement to keep gaze steady, via vestibular nuclei and cranial nerves III, IV and VI.
Vestibular test irrigating the ear canal with warm or cold water to induce nystagmus. Absent response suggests brainstem death or vestibular damage.
Midbrain infarct affecting the oculomotor nerve and cerebral peduncle, causing ipsilateral oculomotor palsy and contralateral hemiparesis.
Midbrain region near the superior colliculus that mediates the pupillary light reflex.
Inhibitory interneurons in the cerebellar granular layer that regulate granule cells.
Brainstem nucleus giving rise to the lateral vestibulospinal tract, which facilitates extensor tone for posture and balance.
Neurons that release dopamine. Loss in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson disease.
Neurons that release acetylcholine. Loss in the nucleus basalis of Meynert is seen in Alzheimer disease.
Output neurons of the retina whose axons form the optic nerve.
Circular channel at the corneoscleral junction draining aqueous humor into the venous system. Blockage raises intraocular pressure.
Parasympathetic ganglion in the orbit relaying fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus to the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle.
Dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light but slowly to accommodation, from damage to the ciliary ganglion. Seen with absent knee reflexes in Holmes-Adie syndrome.
Terminal phase of chronic myeloid leukemia, with transformation into acute leukemia and over 20 percent blasts.
Episodic burning pain, redness and warmth of the extremities, relieved by cooling. Associated with myeloproliferative neoplasms and SCN9A mutations.
Renal proximal tubule proteins that secrete organic acids and drugs such as penicillin. Probenecid inhibits them.
Dengue with plasma leakage, hemorrhage or organ impairment, causing shock and thrombocytopenia.
Alkylating chemotherapy agent used for melanoma and Hodgkin lymphoma (ABVD).
Free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains in urine, seen in multiple myeloma. Not detected by urine dipstick.
Groups of gray matter in the thalamus with specific roles; VPL and VPM relay sensation, LGN vision, MGN hearing.
Central pain with sensory loss after a thalamic stroke, causing burning pain on the opposite side.
Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation, from a dominant parietal lesion (angular gyrus).
Inattention to one side of space, usually the left, after a right parietal lobe lesion.
Bilateral amygdala lesion causing hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity and visual agnosia.
Thalamic nuclei in the Papez circuit linking mammillary bodies and cingulate gyrus; involved in memory.
Infections by picornaviruses such as poliovirus, coxsackievirus and echovirus, spread fecal-orally.
MHC class II gene. Certain alleles are linked to rheumatoid arthritis (DR4) and other autoimmune disease.
Components of gamma-secretase, which cleaves amyloid precursor protein. Mutations cause early-onset familial Alzheimer disease.
Persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, causing cluttered living areas. Classified as a distinct psychiatric disorder.
Repetitive acts performed to reduce anxiety from obsessions, as in OCD.
Neurotoxin that selectively damages substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons, causing parkinsonism. Discovered in contaminated synthetic heroin.
Prion disease with thalamic degeneration, causing progressive untreatable insomnia, autonomic dysfunction and dementia. Autosomal dominant PRNP mutation.
Group of aggressive small round blue cell tumors of neural origin; medulloblastoma is the prototype.
Tumors from neural tube or neural crest-derived cells, such as neuroblastoma, medulloblastoma and Ewing sarcoma.
G-protein-coupled receptor binding CCK, mediating gallbladder contraction and pancreatic secretion.
Gut hormones (GLP-1 and GIP) released after eating that enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion.
Hormone-secreting cells scattered in the gut epithelium, producing gastrin, CCK, secretin, GLP-1 and others.
Enteroendocrine cells in the distal small bowel and colon that secrete GLP-1 and peptide YY.
Pacemaker cells of the gut that generate slow waves driving peristalsis.
Muscular valve at the esophagus start, formed by the cricopharyngeus (inferior pharyngeal constrictor). Zenker diverticulum arises above it.
Glycerol with one fatty acid, the product of triglyceride digestion by pancreatic lipase, absorbed with fatty acids into enterocytes.
MHC class I allele strongly associated with Behcet disease.
White patch in the mouth that cannot be scraped off. Precancerous, associated with tobacco; hairy leukoplakia is EBV-related.
Persistent bad breath, caused by oral bacteria, dental disease, or less often Zenker diverticulum and gastrointestinal disease.
Removing suspected foods and reintroducing them one at a time to identify triggers, used in eosinophilic esophagitis.
Enzyme that deamidates gliadin; the autoantigen of celiac disease. Anti-tTG IgA is the screening test.
Diet excluding wheat, barley and rye; the treatment for celiac disease.
T cells within the gut epithelium, increased in celiac disease.
Structural protein for lipoproteins: B-100 in VLDL, IDL and LDL; B-48 in chylomicrons.
Neuropeptides including substance P, neurokinin A and B, that mediate pain and vomiting. Aprepitant blocks NK1 receptors.
Pain from stimulation of pain receptors by tissue injury, such as somatic or visceral pain, as distinct from neuropathic pain.
Inflammation of the sacroiliac joints, causing low back and buttock pain. Characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis.
Painful inflammation of the sclera often tied to rheumatoid arthritis; deeper and more severe than episcleritis.
Antibodies that block pathogens or toxins from binding host cells, preventing infection.
Colon polyp with finger-like projections and highest malignant potential. Can cause watery diarrhea with hypokalemia.
Whipple procedure removing the pancreatic head, duodenum, gallbladder and bile duct, for pancreatic head cancer.
Adolescent-onset generalized epilepsy with morning myoclonic jerks, tonic-clonic and absence seizures. Treated with valproate.
Divisions of sleep: N1, N2, N3 (slow-wave) and REM, each with EEG patterns. N2 has sleep spindles and K complexes.
Protein encoded by TSC1, a tumor suppressor forming a complex with tuberin to inhibit mTOR. Mutation causes tuberous sclerosis.
Protein encoded by TSC2, a tumor suppressor that inhibits mTOR. Mutation causes tuberous sclerosis.
Flat, uniformly tan-brown skin patches. Six or more over 1.5 cm suggests neurofibromatosis type 1; also McCune-Albright syndrome.
Drugs like cromolyn and nedocromil that prevent mast cell degranulation, used in allergic and asthma prophylaxis.
Refractive error from uneven curvature of the cornea or lens, causing blurred vision at all distances.
Monoclonal antibody fragment blocking VEGF, injected into the eye for wet macular degeneration and diabetic macular edema.
Inner ear structures sensing balance: utricle, saccule and semicircular canals.
Therapist's emotional reaction to a patient, based on the therapist's own past experiences.
Defense mechanism justifying unacceptable behavior with plausible but false explanations.
Child disorder of disturbed relatedness from severe neglect, with emotionally withdrawn behavior toward caregivers.
Cognitive, motor and behavioral decline from HIV infection of the CNS. Previously called AIDS dementia complex.
Focal epilepsy with auras (deja vu, odd smells), automatisms and impaired awareness. Often from hippocampal sclerosis.
Use of sedatives to reduce anxiety and awareness during a procedure while maintaining airway reflexes.
Abnormal behaviors during sleep, such as sleepwalking, night terrors and REM sleep behavior disorder.
Water-soluble conjugate of a drug or bilirubin with glucuronic acid, formed by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase in phase II metabolism.
Melatonin receptor in the suprachiasmatic nucleus that helps regulate sleep timing. Ramelteon acts here.
Slowing of thought and movement, common in depression.
Volatile anesthetic whose metabolism releases fluoride, risking nephrotoxicity.
Volatile inhaled anesthetic; can cause respiratory depression and coronary steal.
Short-acting ester local anesthetic. Metabolized by plasma esterases, forming PABA.
Behavioral therapy gradually confronting feared stimuli to extinguish anxiety response.
Preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance that is slight or invisible to others, causing repetitive behaviors and distress.
Socially recognized exemptions and obligations of ill persons, such as being excused from duties while seeking help.
Caregiver fabricates or induces illness in a dependent, usually a child, to gain attention. Now called factitious disorder imposed on another.
First-generation antihistamine with antiserotonin activity. Used for serotonin syndrome and appetite stimulation.
Tricyclic antidepressant, a secondary amine with mainly norepinephrine reuptake inhibition and fewer anticholinergic effects.
Herbal antidepressant that induces CYP450 and P-glycoprotein, lowering levels of many drugs; can cause serotonin syndrome.
Cluster A disorder of pervasive distrust and suspiciousness of others' motives, without psychosis.
Cluster B disorder of excessive emotionality, attention-seeking, and inappropriate seductiveness.
Cluster B disorder of grandiosity, need for admiration and lack of empathy, with fragile self-esteem.
Freudian part of the psyche that holds moral standards and conscience.
Prodrug of dextroamphetamine used for ADHD and binge eating disorder.
Gamma-hydroxybutyrate used for cataplexy and sleepiness in narcolepsy. CNS depressant.
High-potency typical antipsychotic that blocks D2 receptors. Risk of extrapyramidal symptoms.
Atypical antipsychotic, active metabolite of risperidone, given as long-acting injection (palmitate).
Serotonin receptor mediating platelet aggregation, smooth muscle contraction and hallucinations. Blocked by atypical antipsychotics.
Schizophrenia not responding to at least two antipsychotic trials. Clozapine is the treatment of choice.
Hair standing up from contraction of arrector pili muscles under sympathetic control, seen in cold, fear and opioid withdrawal.
Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease.
Short-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker metabolized by plasma cholinesterase.
Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker cleared by Hofmann elimination, so safe in renal or hepatic failure. Can release histamine.
Prototype nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker; competitive antagonist at nicotinic receptors. Can cause hypotension.
What the body does to a drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.
Elevated bilirubin in newborns, mostly physiologic jaundice. Very high levels risk kernicterus.
Enzyme that converts acetaldehyde to acetate in alcohol metabolism. Inhibited by disulfiram; deficiency causes flushing.
Cell surface receptor that takes up iron-bound transferrin. Upregulated in iron deficiency.
Eye exam using a bright slit of light and microscope to view the front of the eye. Used to detect Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Copper chelator used for Wilson disease, especially in penicillamine intolerance.
Bacteria with thin walls and an outer membrane that need oxygen, such as Pseudomonas and Neisseria.
Adhesion molecule (CD31) on endothelium and leukocytes, mediating transmigration of leukocytes through vessel walls.
External and internal obliques form the lateral abdominal wall, forming the inguinal canal borders.
Protrusion of bowel through an abnormal opening within the abdomen, such as after gastric bypass. Can cause obstruction.
Part of the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor that remains attached to IgA after transport, protecting it from digestion.
Adhesion molecule on leukocytes that mediates rolling on endothelium and lymphocyte homing to lymph nodes.
Elimination of self-reactive lymphocytes by apoptosis, key to central tolerance.
Gene cluster encoding MHC proteins that present antigens to T cells. Located on chromosome 6.
Compatibility of tissues between donor and recipient, determined by HLA antigens.
Class I MHC molecule presenting antigens to CD8 T cells; ligand for natural killer cell KIR receptors.
Autoimmune regulator, a transcription factor in thymic epithelium that expresses self antigens for negative selection. Mutation causes APS type 1.
Immune destruction of multiple endocrine glands. Type 1 (AIRE mutation) causes candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and adrenal failure; type 2 (Schmidt) causes Addison disease with thyroid disease.
Small protein tagged onto other proteins to target them for proteasome degradation.
Antigens such as polysaccharides that activate B cells without T cell help, giving IgM and weak memory.
Protease that cleaves IgG above the hinge into two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment.
Transport of macromolecules across a cell via vesicles from one side to the other, such as IgA through epithelium.
First breast milk after birth, rich in secretory IgA and protective factors.
Epithelial receptor transporting dimeric IgA and pentameric IgM across cells into secretions.
Fc-epsilon receptor on mast cells and basophils; IgE cross-linking triggers degranulation.
Skin test applying allergens under patches for 48 hours to diagnose type IV contact dermatitis.
Protein required to start autophagosome formation. Loss increases cancer risk.
Programmed necrotic cell death regulated by RIPK1, RIPK3 and MLKL, triggered by TNF when caspases are inhibited.
Infection by Nocardia, a partially acid-fast branching filamentous bacterium. Causes pulmonary disease, brain abscesses and cutaneous infection.
Cell surface receptors, such as Fas and TNF receptor, that activate caspases to induce apoptosis.
Drugs such as alteplase that activate plasminogen to dissolve clots, used in stroke, MI and PE.
Controlled cooling after cardiac arrest or neonatal hypoxic-ischemic injury to reduce brain damage.
Inflammasome regulating protein encoded by MEFV. Mutation causes familial Mediterranean fever.
Intracellular innate immune sensors that detect pathogens and form inflammasomes.
Protein of bacterial flagella recognized by TLR5.
Complement fragments C3a, C4a and C5a that trigger mast cell degranulation and vascular permeability.
Adhesion molecules (E-, P- and L-selectin) mediating leukocyte rolling on endothelium.
Endothelial adhesion molecule induced by cytokines that mediates neutrophil rolling.
